Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said trade discussions with the United States will become more intensive. He reported progress in the talks while cautioning that important areas remain unresolved and a deal is not yet done. Carney said some of the red lines in the negotiations had been removed, but others still needed to be addressed. He described the shift in Washington’s position as the United States asking for less and offering more, while stressing that the two sides were not there yet. He also played down the need for formal negotiating rounds. He said it was not always necessary for Canadian trade negotiators to be talking directly with the Office of the US Trade Representative, because good lines of communication were open between the two governments. The comments build on Carney’s update over the weekend, when he said he had held a good conversation with President Donald Trump. He said then that teams from both countries would work over the coming weeks on the outlines of a deal. Trump said last week that he expected a new agreement pretty soon, without giving details. The talks are trying to repair a relationship that deteriorated sharply in August, when negotiations broke down. Trump then imposed a 50% tariff on around $20bn of Canadian goods, equal to roughly 5.5% of Canada’s exports. Ottawa responded with matching tariffs on US products including steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics. Carney’s tone is notably more upbeat than at any point since that breakdown, but his remarks were careful to avoid suggesting an agreement was imminent. His repeated references to unresolved areas and remaining red lines suggest the hardest issues are still on the table, and he gave no timeline for a final deal. The timing adds a political dimension. Americans vote in midterm elections on Tuesday, and trade tensions with Canada are a live issue in states such as Michigan and Maine. The outcome could shape how much room the White House has to compromise in the weeks ahead. The kiwi was already near a cycle low against the Australian dollar after last week’s RBNZ hold, and the gap with a more hawkish RBA now looks set to widen. New Zealand’s unemployment rate rose to 5.7% in the third quarter, above expectations of 5.5%, as employment unexpectedly fell and wage growth slowed, data from Statistics New Zealand showed on Wednesday. Employment declined 0.1% from the previous quarter, against a Reuters poll forecast of a 0.4% gain. The participation rate dropped to 70.4% from 70.6%, below the 70.7% expected. Unemployment rose even though fewer people were looking for work, which points to weak hiring rather than a growing labour force. Earlier figures were also revised lower, with second-quarter employment growth cut to 0.3% from 0.5%. The result runs against bank forecasts that had pointed to a peak in joblessness. Westpac had expected the rate to ease to 5.5%, while ANZ had forecast no change at 5.6%. The June quarter reading of 5.6% was already the highest since 2015. Wage pressures also eased. Private sector wages excluding overtime rose 0.4% in the quarter, below the 0.5% expected, taking annual growth to 2.0% from 2.1%. The data lands at a sensitive moment for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. On 28 October it held the official cash rate at 2.75% in a 4:3 vote, surprising markets that had largely priced a hike. The majority cited weaker than expected inflation, stable inflation expectations and subdued wage growth, and argued that two earlier rate increases needed time to work. Wednesday’s figures support that case on both jobs and pay. Westpac had described today’s release as the first key input before the RBNZ’s next decision on 9 December, while still forecasting a hike at that meeting. The bank cautioned that the move was not a done deal, and a weaker labour market makes that case harder to argue. New Zealand holds a general election on Saturday, adding further uncertainty to the policy outlook ahead of the December meeting. There's always something new to learn about the markets. body: Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. The war on Iran has doubled what Egypt pays for imported LNG, and Cairo is deferring cargoes into 2027 and burning fuel oil in its power plants to hold down the bill. Egypt’s own output fell to 3.63 bcf/d in August as older fields declined faster than new wells came online, and the petroleum ministry has now extended the deadline for bids on 14 exploration blocks meant to reverse that decline to December 14 after companies asked for more time. QatarEnergy has kept its LNG deliveries under force majeure since April, and on October 28 it extended that to the end of December. A government official told Asharq Bloomberg that the price of a single LNG cargo has risen as much as 100% since September, to more than $100 million. Cairo has asked suppliers to push five of its 15 November LNG cargoes into 2027, on top of about 15 cargoes it had already deferred since July. The Petroleum Ministry budgeted $10.1 billion for LNG imports in the fiscal year that began July 1 and had spent $5.8 billion of it by October 6. Egypt has set aside about $1 billion for November cargoes. To cut the bill, EGPC bought six cargoes of high-sulfur fuel oil for delivery in November and December. Egypt’s fuel oil imports have trended higher since April and exceeded 640,000 tons in October. Egyptian gas output has fallen steadily since late 2021. It averaged 4.87 bcf/d in 2024 , then an eight-year low, and about 4 bcf/d in the second half of 2025. In July, Egypt imported more gas than it produced for the first time on record. Imports eased to 3.44 bcf/d in August, still almost half of what the country consumes: 2.24 bcf/d of LNG and 1.20 bcf/d by pipeline from Israel, whose Leviathan partners hold a $35 billion agreement to raise exports to Egypt through 2040. Existing fields lose about 120 mmcfd of output each month, according to the Asharq Bloomberg report. Kpler says new wells and Shell’s (NYSE:SHEL) Mina West field may hold production flat in early 2027 before the decline resumes. Related: IEA Warns Global Gas Crunch Could Last Well into 2027 Petroleum Minister Karim Badawi pledged on September 16 to add about 330 mmcfd of domestic gas by the end of 2026: about 250 mmcfd from the Zohr and West Mina fields in the Mediterranean and about 80 mmcfd from Meleiha in the Western Desert, which he had due by end-September. Eni’s (NYSE:E) Nidoco N-2 well in the Nile Delta started producing about 55 mmcfd in July. BP (NYSE:BP) brought the Fayoum-4 well online in the West Nile Delta on August 31 at about 80 mmcfd, nearly two years early, by drilling sideways from an existing well. Agiba Petroleum, Eni’s joint venture with EGPC, began start-up of the 100 mmcfd Meleiha Phase 2 plant on October 20, three weeks past Badawi’s deadline. Shell’s Mina West field, at about 120 mmcfd, is due to start before year-end. On October 24, the petroleum ministry announced that Chevron’s (NYSE:CVX) Nargis-2 appraisal well in the Mediterranean had encountered up to 35 metres of net gas pay. The well was drilled to more than 5,000 metres, confirmed an extension of the previously discovered reservoir and found an additional gas-bearing layer. MEES estimated the original Nargis discovery, announced in December 2022, at about 3.5 tcf. Chevron operates the concession with 45%, alongside Eni with 30%, Mubadala Energy with 15% and Tharwa Petroleum with 10%. Mubadala bought its stake from Eni in February. On October 5, Chevron signed for the deepwater Lotus block, committing at least $88 million to two exploration wells in 2,000 to 2,800 metres of water, where no deep exploratory well has been drilled. Egypt made nine discoveries in the fiscal year to June, adding about 2.8 tcf of gas reserves. body: What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… While crude oil imports in Asia have reached pre-war levels, imports of refined products remain weak as gasoline and diesel imports from the Middle East have crashed amid reduced refining capacity. Asia’s oil import story these days is a reflection of the global oil markets—crude oil availability has significantly increased since the early summer lows and flows out of the Middle East have largely recovered, but supply of gasoline, and especially diesel, has sharply dropped since the Iran war began at the end of February. Reduced refinery runs in the Middle East, with some refineries still out following Iranian strikes in the early days of the war, have combined with lower refined product flows through the Strait of Hormuz, due to the much more dangerous ship-to-ship transfers of highly inflammable fuels, to slash supply to the market. Russia’s fuel crunch due to Ukrainian strikes on refineries and the lack of Russian diesel exports have compounded the global diesel problem, sending refining margins and retail prices to record highs in the third quarter of the year. The crunch is extending into the fourth quarter, and could last well into 2027, analysts say, as many refineries will have to undergo in the spring long overdue maintenance that has been deferred from this year to maximize production. In this context, crude and product imports in Asia, the world’s biggest oil-importing region, are telling of the state of the global oil market. Asia’s crude oil imports jumped to 26.39 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, up from 24.24 million bpd the month prior, per data by Kpler cited by Reuters’ Asia Commodities and Energy Columnist Clyde Russell. The import levels are estimated at nearly par with the three-month average of 27 million bpd before the Iran war, and up by 39% compared to the lowest level during the conflict so far of 19 million bpd in April, according to the data. Related: IEA Warns Global Gas Crunch Could Last Well into 2027 Asia’s crude imports that have moved through the Strait of Hormuz soared to 7.4 million bpd in October, compared to just 1.6 million bpd in April. Flows through Hormuz en route to Asia are still lagging the pre-war levels of about 13 million bpd, but supply has jumped from Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea port of Yanbu. In recent months, Asian refiners have also materially raised crude oil imports from Russia and the Americas to offset the supply lost at the Strait of Hormuz. In contrast, Asia’s light and middle distillate imports, estimated at about 6.15 million bpd in October by Kpler, were still 10% below pre-war levels. Imports from the Middle East alone remain 18.4% below pre-war volumes, although Asia’s total fuel imports rose from September on the back of increased supply from the Americas and Africa. Gasoline and especially diesel supply remains more restricted than crude oil flows. Since the summer, diesel has been the most distressed barrel in the oil market and soaring refining margins and wholesale and retail prices globally are reflecting this constraint. Despite the recovered crude flows, refineries outside the Middle East and Russia cannot offset the lost capacity, at a time when diesel and other middle distillate demand is rising going into the northern hemisphere winter. body: What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… The world’s biggest oil and gas companies have posted another strong quarter, with just Europe’s top six majors booking a collective $38 billion for the July-to-September quarter. Adding Exxon and Chevron, the figure swells considerably. But the supermajors are in no rush to start spending that windfall. The oil and gas industry is having the exact opposite year to 2020. The war between the United States and Israel, and Iran has pushed oil and gas prices to the highest in years. The war between Russia and Ukraine, meanwhile, has driven refining margins to all-time highs, adding to refining disruption in the Middle East. The combination of developments has driven Exxon’s third-quarter profit up twofold from a year ago, Chevron has booked triple the profit it booked for last year’s third quarter, and BP has reported its highest quarterly profit in its long history. Normally, with these formidable profits, Big Oil should be looking for ways to spend it. Analysts call it a supercycle, and supercycles drive super investments. Not this time, however. This time, Big Oil appears to be focusing on paying down debt, repurchasing stock, and being picky about new investments. Indeed, BP even suspended its share buyback program to cut debt faster—and it has, slashing the total by as much as $10 billion, with the remaining pile now at $13.9 billion. Big Oil appears to be approaching its strong year with a sober mind. Some observers believe this approach to extra-large profits is a sign that Big Oil remains wary of the long-term prospects for their industry. Reuters’ Ron Bousso wrote in a column this week that “Big Oil has so far shied away from major new spending, suggesting the majors do not see today’s market conditions as evidence that the industry’s long-term outlook has improved.” Related: IEA Warns Global Gas Crunch Could Last Well into 2027 This is an interesting suggestion. It would be safe to say that Big Oil companies are quite aware of the fact that the market environment this year is far from the ordinary. It would also be safe to say they are unlikely to be complacent and believe the windfall will never end because that would be childishly naïve, and these are not words one tends to associate with the oil industry. However, the long-term outlook for oil and gas is arguably brighter than it was, say, two years ago. Because the war and its effect on the global economy has demonstrated unequivocally that despite the massive transition push of the past decade, hydrocarbons remain the dominant fuel globally. Not all agree within the industry itself. TotalEnergies, for instance, recently revised its peak oil demand forecast, now expecting that peak between 2035 and 2040. Previously, the company had expected demand to peak after 2040. On the other hand, back in 2024, TotalEnergies expected oil demand to peak after 2030. Meanwhile, commodity trading major Vitol has forecast that oil demand will continue growing until 2040, citing slower than expected global adoption of electric vehicles. Electric vehicles—the electrification of transport—is widely accepted as the leading factor for oil demand decline in the future. It is quite likely the reason Big Oil is being smart with its extra profits this year and not doing business as usual, splurging when the going is good and tightening belts when the cycle hits the trough Still, many forecasts about mass EV adoption and peaking oil demand within a few years turned out to be very far from reality, including a prediction by the International Energy Agency that oil, gas, and coal demand will all start declining before 2030. Her… The American Petroleum Institute (API) estimated that crude oil inventories in the United States fell by 5.267 million barrels in the week ending October 30. In the week prior, US crude oil inventories fell by a staggering 2.031 million barrels. Commercial crude oil inventories excluding the SPR have lost more than 64 million barrels over the last 29 weeks, and 12 million over this year, according to API data, which has been kept in check in part thanks to draws from the SPR. For the week ending October 30, 400,000 barrels of crude oil left the SPR to aid commercial inventories, bringing the total inventory held in the SPR down to 282.2 million barrels —a level that is 432 million barrels shy of maximum capacity. The generally accepted operational minimum for oil in the SPR is between 250-300 million barrels, below which the reserve may find it difficult to pump and process oil efficiently. US production for the week ending Oct 23 rose to 13.992 million bpd , up from 13.269 million bpd in the week prior, and up 348,000 bpd from a year ago. Gasoline inventories rose by 1.427 million during the week ending October 30. In the week prior, gasoline inventories rose by 2.39 million barrels. In the week prior, gasoline inventories were 2% below the five-year average for this time of year, according to the latest EIA data. Distillate inventories fell by 270,000 barrels compared to the 380,000 barrels gained in the week prior. Distillate inventories were already 10% below the five-year average heading into this reporting period, the latest EIA data shows. Cushing inventory—the inventory kept at the delivery hub for the WTI Crude futures contract—gained 511,000 barrels after losing 453,000 barrels in the previous week. body: I-80 Gold (TSX: IAU; NYSE: IAUX) expects annual production in the lower half of its forecast range after worker turnover slowed mining in Nevada, even as the company’s next underground operation approaches a year-end start. The stock dropped. Toronto-based i-80 maintained its 40,000–50,000 oz. outlook but flagged delayed access to high-grade ore at Granite Creek and a processing change that shifts some gold from the Archimedes mine into early 2027. Production mining at Archimedes and the refurbishment of the Lone Tree processing plant remain on schedule, i-80 said in its quarterly update Monday. “The contractor workforce has since been restored to previous staffing levels to support planned mining rates following an adjustment to contractor compensation structure,” chief operating officer Paul Chawrun said in the release. The setbacks highlight the operating demands behind i-80’s plan to lift annual gold output to 150,000–200,000 oz. starting in 2028. Its Lone Tree restart would allow the company to process its own refractory ore, which requires treatment to release gold trapped in sulphide minerals, and retain more of the margin now paid to third parties. title: Will the Fed raise interest rates this year? Divided economists weigh in - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
body: The central bank has held interest rates steady five consecutive times. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh this week struck a combative tone about inflation, but the central bank opted against deploying its most powerful weapon: An interest rate hike . "The path to central bank heaven means delivering on our remit," Warsh told reporters in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday afternoon. "This is the right team to win the battle against high inflation." The remarks came minutes after the central bank issued its decision to hold interest rates steady for a fifth consecutive time, though pressure for a rate hike seemed to be building within its ranks. Three of the 12 members on the Fed's policymaking board voted in favor of a rate hike, marking the largest number of dissenters casting ballots in the same direction since 2016. After the announcement, economists appeared as divided as the policymakers, underscoring the uncertain prospects for a rate hike by the end of this year. Some analysts told ABC News they expect a rate increase as soon as the Fed's next meeting in September, pointing to risks posed by price increases as global oil shortage shows little sign of letting up. Others cast doubt on whether the Fed will raise rates at all over the remainder of 2026, noting an apparent willingness on the part of Warsh to let the market push borrowing costs higher without a nudge from the central bank. "Uncertainty and volatility are a feature and not a bug," Joseph Brusuelas, global economist at RSM, said in a note to investors about Warsh's stated preference that investors respond to economic events rather than Fed policy statements. "This has turned out to be anything but a boring and uneventful summer," Brusuelas added. The Iran war triggered a historic oil shortage that drove up fuel costs and catapulted inflation to a three-year high in May, the same month Warsh took the helm of the central bank. A preliminary peace agreement in June offered up some relief , but a burst of on-again, off-again fighting in recent weeks has caused crude prices to rise again. Elevated price increases pose a challenge for central bankers eager to beat back price hikes. In theory, the Fed could raise interest rates in an effort to cool off prices, but the move risks a slowdown of hiring. Fortunately, hiring has proven largely resilient, despite increased costs borne by shoppers and businesses. Odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in September stand at 63%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool , a measure of investor sentiment. Odds of a rate hike by the end of the year stand at 83%. "I do think we're going to see a rate hike. Maybe not at the next meeting but at some time in 2026," Rebel Cole, a professor of finance at Florida Atlantic University who formerly worked at the Federal Reserve, told ABC News. "Inflation won't come down until oil prices do. The Fed is boxed in." Some economists, by contrast, questioned whether the Fed would raise interest rates over the remainder of the year. The Fed holds little capacity to address inflation driven by supply shortages, such as the current oil shock, Brusuelas said. Higher interest rates would instead reduce demand as shoppers and businesses weather expensive borrowing costs. The Fed may instead expect inflation to fall once oil supply returns, Brusuelas said. "We think that the nature of the supply shock and the Fed's tendency to look through such shocks implies that the Fed has the space to keep the policy rate on hold," Brusuelas added. Warsh, meanwhile, has said he wants to let investors set the cost of borrowing in the market for short- and long-term bonds, instead of taking a strong hand himself through public statements or policy prescriptions. body: The third quarter delivered sharply different outcomes across financial markets. Stocks reached record highs, while rising interest rates challenged bonds. Beneath the surface, strong artificial intelligence-related earnings, elevated energy prices and higher borrowing costs shaped performance and reinforced the importance of diversification, quality and a long-term perspective. The S&P 500 gained 2.3% during the quarter, but performance varied considerably across sectors. Energy, technology and health care led the market, while rate-sensitive areas such as utilities and real estate came under pressure. Small-cap stocks also struggled as higher energy prices and borrowing costs presented additional headwinds. International developed markets were roughly flat, while emerging markets experienced a modest decline. Fixed income faced a more challenging environment. Although the repricing created near-term losses, it also raised starting yields to more attractive levels, potentially improving future income and return opportunities. 1 Record stock prices and elevated bond yields may appear to send conflicting signals. In our view, both reflect an economy that has remained stronger than expected. Healthy corporate profits have continued to support equities, with earnings growth broadening across sectors. At the same time, bond yields have risen as inflation remains elevated, fiscal deficits increase, and investors adjust to higher interest-rate expectations. So far, corporate earnings growth has been strong enough to absorb the effects of higher interest rates, and we believe that bond yields should begin to moderate over the next year. For the Australian dollar and commodities, the slightly firmer manufacturing output is a modest offset, but the softer services reading gives little reason to expect a stronger demand impulse from China. --- Chinese service firms are still finding customers and hiring staff, but they are cutting prices to do it while their own costs climb, a squeeze that shows up in profits before it shows up in growth. China’s services sector kept growing in October but at a slower pace, a private survey showed on Wednesday. Firms cut prices to win business even though their own costs rose at the fastest rate in five months. The RatingDog China General Services PMI, compiled by S&P Global, fell to 50.8 in October from 51.6 in September. The reading stayed above the 50 mark that separates expansion from contraction, but it showed the slowest growth in activity in three months. Firms pointed to operational constraints as a factor behind the slowdown. Demand held up better than the headline suggests. New business continued to rise at a solid pace, little changed from September, extending a run of growth that began in January 2023. Firms credited wider customer bases and successful promotional efforts. New export orders rose for a sixth straight month, the longest stretch since 2024, though growth eased and was marginal. Hiring picked up. Employment rose for a sixth month, and at a faster pace than in September, as firms took on both full- and part-time staff. The extra workers, along with what firms described as efficiency gains from AI, helped reduce backlogs of work for the first time in a year. Pricing remains the main concern. Average selling prices fell for a second month as firms discounted to cope with fierce competition, although the pace of discounting eased from September. At the same time, input cost inflation hit a five-month high, driven by higher labour, raw material and oil costs, with some firms also citing social security payments. That combination points to pressure on profit margins. Business confidence stayed positive but slipped to a three-month low, as firms worried about rising costs and competition. A separate composite index, which combines manufacturing and services, fell to 52.0 from 52.4, the slowest rise in private sector output in three months. Faster growth in manufacturing output was not enough to offset the softer services expansion. RatingDog founder Yao Yu said that steady new business and stronger hiring underpinned growth at the start of the fourth quarter, but that renewed discounting and rising costs were weighing on profitability. The fall in two-year swaps supports that reading. With the RBA still leaning hawkish, the widening policy gap leaves NZD/AUD vulnerable to further weakness. The election is the next risk: a Labour-led win would bring the prospect of a dual mandate, which markets would likely read as tilting the RBNZ toward easier policy over time. Inflation expectations surveys later this month are the next test of whether the RBNZ’s hawks can still make their case. New Zealand’s jobs data missed on every measure, handing the RBNZ a reason to stay on hold and the opposition a fresh line of attack days before the vote. New Zealand’s unemployment rate climbed to an 11-year high in the third quarter, data released earlier on Wednesday showed. The New Zealand dollar has traded lower since, as markets weigh the outlook for interest rates and Saturday’s general election. To recap, the jobless rate rose to 5.7% in the three months to September, the highest since 2015, according to Statistics New Zealand. Economists polled by Reuters had expected 5.5%, as had the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Employment fell 0.1% from the previous quarter, against forecasts of a 0.4% rise, and the participation rate slipped to 70.4%, below the 70.7% expected. Wage growth also slowed. Private sector labour costs excluding overtime rose 0.4% in the quarter, down from 0.7% in the previous three months, taking annual growth to 2.0% from 2.1%. The figures land in the final days of a tight election campaign, Reuters reported, with an Ipsos poll this week showing inflation and the cost of living as voters’ top concern. Labour’s finance spokesperson, Barbara Edmonds, said the data was a damning judgement on Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s handling of the economy. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said the numbers reflected the effect of uncertainty and showed the need to stay with the government’s plan, which she said was rebuilding the economy. Markets read the data as reducing pressure on the central bank to resume rate rises. The kiwi dipped on the release before steadying around $0.56, Reuters reported, and has since drifted lower. Two-year swap rates fell about 6 basis points to around 3.78%. The RBNZ surprised markets last week by holding its official cash rate at 2.75%. It said it wanted time to judge the effect of two earlier hikes, while signalling further increases were still likely. Economists at one local bank said the weakening labour market made that decision look increasingly justified, and suggested further hikes may not be needed if the trend continued. The election adds a further policy question. Labour has pledged to return the RBNZ to a dual mandate covering both price stability and maximum sustainable employment, rather than its current single focus on inflation. title: Gold Shatters $5,000 With Its Fastest Weekly Surge Yet - Startup Fortune
body: Gold didn't just cross $5,000 an ounce this week. It blew past every major bank's 2026 forecast in the process, and did it faster than the rally that got it there. Spot gold hit a record $5,594.82 an ounce this week before settling near $5,546, marking a ninth straight record-setting session and a weekly gain of more than 10%. That single week beats what most stock portfolios return in a year. Gold is now up more than 27% in 2026, stacked on a 64% rally in 2025, according to market data reported by Reuters and Kitco. What makes this leg different isn't only the level. It's the pace. When Reuters polled 30 analysts and traders for its annual gold survey, the median 2026 forecast came in at $4,746.50 an ounce, the highest consensus the poll has recorded since it began in 2012. Gold has already blown past that number by hundreds of dollars with two months still left in the year. Goldman Sachs' $5,400 target, once treated as the conservative anchor among big banks, is behind the market too. JPMorgan's $6,300 call and UBS's range of $6,200 to $7,200 now read as the realistic zone, not the stretch case. Three forces are pushing this. China's central bank, the PBOC, added roughly 21 tonnes of gold in September alone, its largest single monthly purchase since 2023 and its 23rd consecutive month of buying, according to data reported by Kitco and the World Gold Council. Globally, central banks bought 288.9 tonnes of gold in the second quarter of 2026, up 62% from a year earlier. That's not speculative money chasing a chart. It's reserve managers in China, Poland and elsewhere making a multi-year bet to diversify away from the dollar. The dollar itself is the second leg. A weaker greenback makes gold cheaper for buyers holding other currencies, and the dollar has been sliding as traders price in further Federal Reserve rate cuts. The third leg is the strangest one: a US government shutdown has knocked out the normal flow of economic data, leaving the Fed, and everyone watching it, flying partly blind. That blackout hasn't calmed anyone down. It's done the opposite, feeding rate-cut bets and safe-haven buying at once. Gold is sliding toward $4,100 an ounce even after Iran's Revolutionary Guard fired missiles at a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, as a stronger dollar and rising oil-driven inflation fears offset safe-haven demand. Silver, meanwhile, is holding near $60 and outpacing gold for most of 2026, with J.P. Morgan and Reuters analysts eyeing $80 by... - why gold prices falling geopolitical tensions - gold safe haven trade breakdown Retail buyers should pause before piling in at $5,500. Technical readings on gold's monthly chart are now the most overbought they've been since 1980, according to analysis cited by FX Street, a signal that has historically preceded sharp pullbacks even inside a longer bull run. The 2025 rally, explosive as it was, played out over twelve months. This leg added more than 10% in a single week. Momentum like that rarely runs in a straight line. The floor isn't about to drop out. The central banks haven't shown any sign of slowing, and a government that still can't publish reliable jobs or inflation data isn't about to give markets a reason to stop hedging. But there's a real difference between gold climbing because reserve managers are quietly repositioning over years and gold jumping 10% in a week because retail traders are chasing a chart that has already outrun every major bank's forecast. The first is a trend. The second is the stretch of a rally where whoever buys last usually pays the most and holds the bag longest when it cools. Goldman, JPMorgan and UBS all raised their numbers through the year and gold still beat them. summary: It was driven by energy inflation, which surged above 20% in October.
body: Inflation in the euro area jumped to a three-year high of 4% in October, a flash estimate showed on Wednesday. The reading is in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and was up from 3.8% in September . Officials said the increase was largely due to surging energy costs, with energy inflation rising to 20.8% from 18.9% in September. Europe, a net energy importer, is vulnerable to external energy shocks and has seen prices rise steadily since the start of the Iran war. October marked the first time inflation in the euro zone has hit or exceeded the 4% threshold since Sept. 2023's reading of 4.3%. Inflation also varied across the 21 euro zone economies, with Lithuania recording the hottest inflation rate of 6.1% while Malta's was the lowest at 2.3%. All euro zone countries saw inflation hold above the European Central Bank's 2% target. The euro was up 0.6% against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday morning, although the greenback fell against a basket of major currencies as counting continued in the U.S. midterm elections, while the yield on the 10-year German bund — broadly seen as a benchmark for euro zone bonds — was marginally higher. Policymakers said underlying inflation and wages were broadly stable, despite inflation sitting at a three-year high. The European Central Bank kept its key interest rate at 2.5% last month, following a hike of 25 basis points in September. Shortly before Wednesday's inflation print, markets were pricing in a 71.8% chance of a hike at the ECB's final meeting of the year in December. Following the data release, markets were pricing in more than a 72% chance of rates rising. Robert Mertens, global capital markets senior analyst at Validus Risk Management, cautioned that "ongoing turmoil in the French bond market is placing constraints on ECB policy" and the bank's capacity to get inflation under control. "Should we see an easing in French political unrest, the ECB could potentially pursue a more aggressive hiking path," he said. "If the ECB can deploy more aggressive tightening relative to the Federal Reserve, we would see increased Euro support and upside versus the Dollar."

title: Marubeni Raises FY2027 Net Profit Forecast to ¥630 Billion on Copper, Chemicals - finance.biggo.com
body: Marubeni (8002.T) announced on November 4 that it has raised its consolidated net profit forecast (under International Financial Reporting Standards) for the fiscal year ending March 2027 to ¥630 billion (approximately $4.0 billion), up 16% from the prior year and above its previous guidance of ¥580 billion. The company expects a record-high profit. The revision incorporates higher earnings from its Chilean copper business and petrochemicals trading. The forecast also exceeded the market consensus average, and the annual dividend forecast was raised by ¥10 to ¥125 (approximately $0.79) from the previous ¥115 (approximately $0.73). For the April-September 2026 period, consolidated net profit rose 11% year-on-year to ¥338 billion (approximately $2.1 billion), marking a record high for a first half. Revenue increased 23% to ¥5.18 trillion (approximately $32.9 billion). Rising resource prices boosted earnings in the mining and smelting segment, while non-resource businesses such as chemicals, trading, and lifestyle and agriculture-related operations also grew. Adjusted net profit, excluding one-time factors, rose 45% to ¥318 billion (approximately $2.0 billion). The company's full-year adjusted net profit outlook was raised to ¥600 billion (approximately $3.8 billion) from the previous ¥540 billion (approximately $3.4 billion), also a record high. Improved earnings in the metals business driven by a market recovery were the main factor behind the upward revision, with copper mines and aluminum-related operations contributing. Note: Full-year net profit year-on-year change is based on company disclosure. First half refers to April-September 2026. The revised net profit forecast exceeded the market consensus average of ¥620.2 billion (approximately $3.9 billion) compiled by QUICK Consensus. It also surpassed the average of ¥614.5 billion (approximately $3.9 billion) from 11 analysts in a separate survey, making it guidance that topped market expectations. However, in stock market trading on November 4 following the announcement, Marubeni shares at one point fell 3% to ¥4,676. The positive news had already been priced in to some extent, and cautious views on the outlook for resource prices are believed to have weighed on the stock. The environment surrounding major Japanese trading houses is being supported by a recovery in non-ferrous metal prices such as copper and aluminum. Marubeni has stated its policy of expanding earnings through both resource and non-resource businesses, and the latest upward revision reflects the resilience of its chemicals and trading operations. body: Oil prices took a leg down on Monday as the outlook for potential diplomatic breakthroughs in the Middle East strengthened just a day before midterm elections that could represent a pivotal moment for the Iran war. Futures on Brent crude ( BZ=F ), the international benchmark, shed around 7.9% to trade below $105 per barrel, while those on US WTI crude ( CL=F ) lost 7.5% to hold near $96. Oil futures initially began to move downward on Monday after Axios reported that, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pressed the White House for a forceful round of strikes on Iran, President Trump has said he wants to give diplomacy with Tehran another shot . The reporting from Axios aligns with public statements in recent days from President Trump, where he has said the US won't strike Iran after the midterms. However, reporting by national outlets in recent weeks has indicated that the US military has briefed Trump on options for a major reescalation after the midterms, when the risk of political backlash against the president will be lessened. Adding to the downward pressure on oil prices Monday, leaders in Tehran said contact with the US over negotiations to end the war is continuing , Reuters reported, as talks between Iran and Qatari mediators have produced proposal language but no breakthrough agreement. "Consultations through mediators are very intensive," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in comments to the state-run media outlet IRNA. "We have ‌presented our conditions and proposals and everything depends on the political rationality of Washington." Leaders in China and Russia both spoke out against a full-fledged resumption of hostilities on Monday, in comments from their foreign ministries. China is a major buyer of energy from the Gulf region, and after largely staying out of the conflict through its first several months, it has engaged more directly in recent weeks. In Russia, the war in Iran has added to the nation's domestic fuel shortage, caused largely by strikes on oil refineries by the Ukrainian military and international sanctions levied against Moscow. President Vladimir Putin reportedly spoke with Iranian security lead official Mohsen Rezaei on Monday , per Reuters. Even so, the diplomatic headlines haven't yet tempered predictions on Wall Street that oil prices will remain higher for longer. Goldman Sachs analysts led by Daan Struyven said on Monday that they now expect Brent prices to average $105 per barrel in December, up from a previous forecast of $90. They see Brent contracts averaging $88 per barrel in 2027, up from a prior $80 forecast. If the White House were to restart strikes on Iran, the US military would likely target nuclear stores buried in Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, missile facilities near the Strait of Hormuz, or broader civilian energy infrastructure such as power plants, the Goldman analysts said. Such a move would likely incite a response from Iran that could include impacts on oil infrastructure in the Gulf region, further pressuring an already strained oil market. Elevated risks of escalation, beliefs that a lasting US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough will be hard to achieve quickly, and historical norms showing that past oil supply shocks have lasted for years with long-term damage all suggest the oil risk premium will stay higher for longer, the analysts said. title: Goldman Sachs hikes oil forecasts on ‘substantial’ risks to supply - BusinessWorld Online
body: GOLDMAN SACHS Group, Inc. raised oil-price forecasts for the year-end and 2027 on elevated risks to supplies, joining other banks in hiking their outlooks a f ter months of war in the Middle East. Brent is now seen at $105 a barrel in December, up from a previous estimate of $90, and will average $88 next year, 10% more than seen before, analysts including Daan Struyven and Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby said in a note, which also increased forecasts for US oil marker West Texas Intermediate. “Substantial downside supply risks are likely to sustain a large, near-term risk premium,” the analysts wrote. The markets are assigning “increasing weight to escalation after the Nov. 3 US midterms and subsequent potential weakness in Mideast supply,” they added in the Nov. 1 report. Global benchmark Brent rallied 14% in October, hitting a six-month high, even as crude supplies from the Middle East rebounded close to pre-war levels. The gains came on concern that hostilities between the US and Iran may fl are up again after the midterm elections, with President Donald Trump repeatedly hinting that he may resume airstrikes. For his part, Iran’s supreme leader has ordered his top commanders to prepare for renewed confrontation. Intensified shipping attacks and damage to infrastructure were among factors that could trigger further price gains, the analysts said, while also highlighting risks from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “With the timing and location of disruptions nearly impossible to predict, our base case now includes a 1-million-barrel-per-day global supply disruption allowance in 2027.” Beyond its core view, Goldman also sketched bullish and bearish frameworks for 2027 with prices spanning a range of about $70, highlighting the challenges facing forecasters as they grapple with a wide range of potential outcomes. In the bank’s upside scenario, Brent may average $130 next year if Persian Gulf output remains 3.5 million barrels a day below last year’s average, the analysts said. But in the downside version, marked by a faster recovery in regional output, futures “might decline into the $60s,” they said. In recent weeks, Morgan Stanley raised its forecast for Dated Brent — a key physical price — to $105 a barrel for the fourth quarter, while ANZ Group Holdings Ltd. hiked its year-end outlook for Brent futures to the same figure. Most-active contracts fell below $110 in Monday’s trade. — Bloomberg

title: How do midterm candidates plan to fight inflation? Economists evaluate their proposals - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
body: The final sprint to Tuesday's midterm elections has kicked up a flurry of headlines about attack ads slung by candidates and verbal jabs thrown by current and former occupants of the White House. An issue crucial to households' bank account balances, however, has preoccupied voters for the duration of campaign season: Affordability. The Iran war set off a monthslong surge of inflation as fuel prices climbed in response to unrest in the Middle East, U.S. government data shows. In response to rising prices, a jump in bond yields has pushed up rates for loans like credit cards and mortgages, threatening to worsen the financial crunch . Candidates for Congress have voiced a range of proposals meant to address the price woes, including tax cuts, an easing of regulations, a removal of tariffs and an end to the Iran war. Some economists spoke to ABC News about whether the proposals could cool off inflation. Analysts praised some policies and criticized others, but they all acknowledged that no single measure could dramatically shift the price picture, at least anytime soon. Here's what to know about some affordability proposals made on the campaign trail, according to experts: The Iran war triggered a rise of inflation earlier this year as a historic oil supply shortage pushed up prices for gasoline, groceries and other essentials. Some candidates, mostly Democrats, have proposed an end to the Iran war as a means of dialing back price hikes. "We were promised no new foreign wars, but here we are, 185 days into a new foreign war and Nebraskans are paying the price," Dan Osborn, an independent candidate for U.S. Senate in Nebraska, said at a debate in September. On his campaign website , Osborn calls for "ending the wars that drive up prices and costs the lives of American servicemen and women," pointing specifically to the Iran war. When asked last month how he would bring down prices, Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who is up for re-election, vowed to "end this disastrous war in Iran." Analysts who spoke to ABC News attributed elevated prices for gasoline and some other goods to ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has damaged oil infrastructure and forced firms to take up costly means of transporting crude. The last time Nigeria produced an average of more than 1.7 million bpd of crude and condensate for a full month was in July 2025. Nigeria has struggled to pump to its OPEC+ quota in recent years as sabotage often led to force majeure at major export streams. However, with a recent crackdown on oil theft and sabotage in the Niger Delta, Nigeria has managed to increase crude production and aims for further growth by 2030. title: Copper’s biggest new mine stumbles again as costs soar
summary: A second production downgrade at Ivanhoe Mines’ Kamoa-Kakula delays its recovery as a rival US expansion advances toward 2030 output.
body: Robert Friedland’s Ivanhoe Mines (TSX: IVN) has cut its 2027 copper production forecast for Kamoa-Kakula in the Democratic Republic of Congo for the second time this year while raising costs and extending the recovery of the world’s largest new copper mine developed in recent years. The Canadian miner, which released the update after markets closed Tuesday , now expects to produce 300,000 to 350,000 tonnes of copper next year, down from 380,000 to 420,000 tonnes. This removes 75,000 tonnes from the plan at the midpoint. Its target stood at 500,000 to 540,000 tonnes before a more cautious mine plan emerged in March. Ivanhoe also raised its 2027 cash cost (C1) guidance to $2.50 to $3.00 per pound from $2.10 to $2.50, citing prolonged high diesel prices, lower ore grades and reduced production. “The revised production and cost guidance over the short term reflects a disciplined approach to the ongoing turnaround at Kamoa-Kakula, prioritizing operational stability, mining flexibility and the sustainable recovery of annualized copper production to approximately 500,000 tonnes,” Friedland, Ivanhoe’s founder and co-chairman, said in the statement. The downgrade highlights the difficulty of restoring major copper operations even as miners race to bring new supply to market. While Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE: FCX) has approved an expansion at its Bagdad mine in Arizona targeting additional production in 2030, Kamoa-Kakula’s recovery is taking longer than expected. “The path back to about 500,000 tonnes per year has become longer, more capital intensive and more dependent on future execution,” TD Cowen analyst Craig Hutchison wrote in a note Tuesday. He downgraded Ivanhoe to hold from buy and slashed his target price to C$9 ($6.42) from C$14. Ivanhoe lowered the expected steady-state annual production capacity of Kamoa-Kakula’s existing Phase 1, 2 and 3 concentrators to 400,000 to 450,000 tonnes as it prepares to introduce shallow open-pit mining alongside its underground operations. The company plans to begin stripping waste rock from two high-grade starter pits in the first quarter of 2027, with first ore expected in the third quarter. The new mining approach is intended to improve flexibility while the underground Kakula mine recovers. That turnaround has suffered another setback. Ivanhoe now expects production mining on the eastern side of Kakula to restart in late March 2028, rather than late 2027, following further geological and engineering work. Kamoa-Kakula produced 76,401 tonnes of copper in saleable products during the third quarter, up from 64,328 tonnes in the preceding three months. Full-year 2026 output is expected to reach approximately 290,000 tonnes. The company also reduced the upper end of its 2026 capital spending forecast by $200 million, deferring that expenditure to 2027. Next year’s spending guidance now stands at $950 million to $1.15 billion, excluding an estimated $100 million to $200 million for open-pit pre-stripping. Ivanhoe plans to begin detailed engineering for a Phase 4 concentrator expansion in the first quarter of 2027, aiming to lift annual copper production capacity to approximately 500,000 tonnes. The expansion has not yet received project approval. Ivanhoe estimates construction would take 18 to 24 months after approval, with an updated life-of-mine plan scheduled for March 2027. title: Freeport approves $4.5 billion Bagdad copper expansion
summary: By greenlighting the Arizona mine expansion Freeport-McMoRan aims to double copper production amid rising demand.
body: Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE: FCX) has approved a $4.5-billion expansion of its Bagdad mine in Arizona that would more than double copper output, bolstering domestic supply as Washington seeks to lessen China’s dominance of metals processing. The investment would lift the site’s annual copper production to more than 400 million lb., an increase of about 225 million lb., making Bagdad the second-largest copper mine in the United States behind Freeport’s Morenci operation. Molybdenum output would climb by 12 million lb. annually to more than 20 million lb., the company said Wednesday . The expansion marks “an important step in advancing Freeport’s US copper growth strategy,” CEO Kathleen Quirk said. Initial production is targeted for mid-2030 following about three-and-a-half years of construction. The project would add concentrating facilities capable of processing 115,000 tonnes of ore daily, alongside a crusher, conveyor and expanded infrastructure. Freeport anticipates a roughly 20% reduction in long-term unit net cash costs. “The largely anticipated approval comes amid healthy copper prices, with capital intensity, production expectations and timing consistent with prior communications,” BMO Capital Markets mining analyst Katja Jancic said in a note. Capital costs are about $1 billion, or 29%, above the $3.5 billion estimate prepared in 2023. In its third-quarter filing last week , Freeport attributed the increase to cost escalation, changes in project scope and revised estimates following additional engineering. Project economics are supported at a copper price of about $4 per lb., Freeport says. The expanded operation to benefit from economies of scale, modernized operating practices and lower costs over the long term, the company added. Bagdad’s existing reserves support more than 80 years of operations, providing a substantial base for the investment. The expansion also strengthens an integrated domestic business. Freeport manages seven US copper operations and operates a smelter and rod mill in Miami, Arizona, plus a refinery and rod mill in El Paso, Texas. Its growth strategy includes recovering additional copper from existing leach stockpiles using additives and heat. Washington has sought to speed up investment through faster permitting and financial support. President Donald Trump’s March 2025 minerals order directed agencies to expedite priority projects and expanded access to Defence Production Act authorities to support domestic mineral production, explicitly including copper. The measures cover mining, processing, refining and smelting. The Trump administration has framed copper supply as a national-security concern because of its use in military equipment, electrical infrastructure and manufacturing. China controls more than half of global copper smelting capacity, the White House says. America’s immediate import dependence largely involves other suppliers. Net imports supplied 57% of US refined-copper consumption in 2025, according to data from the US Geological Survey. Chile accounted for 68% of refined imports during 2021–24, followed by Canada at 16%. Freeport shares dropped 0.3% to $61.60 Wednesday morning in US trading, valuing the company at about $86 billion. The stock has traded between $38.54 and $80.24 in the past year. The investment comes as the EU steps up efforts to cut their dependence on Chinese rare earths and magnets.

title: B2Gold’s $740 million Gramalote faces key permit test
summary: Regulators will weigh proposed design changes as the Canadian miner targets construction in 2027 and first gold in 2029.
body: Colombia’s environmental regulator will hold a public hearing on Nov. 10 to consider changes to the permit for B2Gold’s (TSX: BTO) $740-million Gramalote gold project, a key step toward construction of the proposed open-pit mine in Antioquia. The National Environmental Licensing Authority (ANLA) has briefed more than 500 residents of San Roque and Yolombó, the municipalities near the project. The hearing will allow communities and other interested parties to raise concerns before the regulator decides whether to approve the proposed changes. B2Gold submitted its application in April 2026 to revise an environmental licence granted in 2015 for a larger mining operation. The Canadian company has since scaled back the project and proposed relocating its processing plant and some supporting infrastructure. The review comes as Colombia seeks to revive mining investment following a steep decline in foreign capital inflows. Approval would clear a major regulatory hurdle for Gramalote, although the project remains exposed to permitting and development risks before its planned start of production in late 2029. B2Gold’s 2025 feasibility study estimates initial capital costs of $740 million and an 11-year mine life, with the processing plant expected to operate for 13 years. The company forecasts average annual gold production of 227,000 oz. during the first five years, declining to an average of 177,000 oz. over the full operating period. B2Gold expects to secure environmental approval in January 2027 and begin construction the following month, subject to regulatory clearance. The project contains indicated mineral resources of 155.6 million tonnes grading 0.70 gram gold per tonne, equivalent to approximately 3.52 million oz. Inferred resources total 120.9 million tonnes grading 0.52 gram gold per tonne, containing about 2 million oz., according to the company. B2Gold also estimates post-construction capital spending of $444 million over the project’s life, including $376 million in sustaining capital. The company gained full ownership of Gramalote in 2023 after acquiring AngloGold Ashanti’s (JSE: ANG) (NYSE: AU) 50% interest. The permitting process comes as Colombia’s government attempts to reverse a sharp contraction in foreign mining investment, which fell 88% to $178 million in 2025 from $1.51 billion in 2022, according to the Ministry of Mines and Energy. President Abelardo de la Espriella’s administration has proposed measures to encourage investment, including repealing special mining districts and Food Production Protection Areas (APPA). The government’s Economic Rescue Bill , submitted to Congress on Oct. 29, also includes a Single Regime to Generate Business Stability (RUGE), intended to improve conditions for private investment. Deputy Mines Minister Luis Madriñán said the mining industry would need to expand by at least 10% to support the government’s ambition of 6% economic growth, underscoring the importance of attracting private capital. Madriñán also identified copper as a major opportunity for Colombia’s mining industry, signalling the government’s interest in expanding beyond its established gold and coal sectors. The investment comes as the EU steps up efforts to cut their dependence on Chinese rare earths and magnets.

body: How Analyst Downgrades Affect Crypto Exchange Stocks, Not Tokens When an analyst downgrades crypto exchange stocks, the rating applies to a company: its revenue, costs, competition, and valuation. A token is a different animal. Its price comes from supply, demand, liquidity, and wider market mood, not from a bank's view of an exchange's profit forecast. The two can move together, because exchanges earn more when trading is busy, but a downgrade is not a verdict on any coin. A story about a downgrade appears next to a story about a price drop, and readers join the dots. Exchange shares also tend to rise and fall with crypto sentiment, so the link feels obvious. The connection is real but indirect. Exchanges make money from trading activity, custody, interest, and other services, and all of those depend partly on how excited people are about crypto . When prices and volumes sag, revenue forecasts usually sag too. Readers who follow crypto news Today we will see the same names appear in both kinds of stories. Two recent examples show how analysts think about crypto exchange stocks. In late October 2026, a research firm trimmed its target on a large US exchange while keeping a positive rating. According to a report, the reasons were weaker trading volumes and a stalled recovery, balanced by growth expected from prediction markets and derivatives. The analysts also said they no longer assumed any bullish crypto price action in their estimates, which is a statement about modeling, not a forecast for tokens. The cut is also covered in Coinbase Stock News . In early November 2026, a large investment bank went further and downgraded the same exchange to a negative rating with a sharply lower target. A report on the downgrade cited a crowded field of competitors, weaker earnings estimates, and quarterly results where most of the profit gain came from marks on crypto holdings, not from operations. That report did not describe any effect on bitcoin. A stock rating is a claim about future profit. A token has no profit statement. Several things separate them: Different drivers, Shares respond to earnings, margins, and competition. Tokens respond to adoption, liquidity, regulation, issuance, and market flows. Different holders, Stocks sit with institutions, funds, and brokerage customers. Tokens are held by traders, long-term holders, and protocols. Different information, A listed company publishes audited filings with the SEC . Many tokens publish nothing comparable. Different calendars, Stock markets close. Token markets don't. Different risk, A stock can fall while the token's business trades rise, and the reverse is also possible. body: Robert Friedland’s Ivanhoe Mines (TSX: IVN; US-OTC: IVPAF) has cut next year’s copper production outlook at Kamoa-Kakula by 19% as recovery work at the flood-hit operation in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) takes longer than expected. The stock hit a four-year low. Vancouver-based Ivanhoe now expects 300,000 to 350,000 tonnes of copper in saleable products in 2027, down from 380,000 to 420,000 tonnes, according to a statement issued Tuesday after the close of trading. This year’s forecast has narrowed to about 290,000 tonnes, the bottom of the miner’s previous 290,000-to-310,000-tonne range. The setback means Ivanhoe needs another expansion to reach the copper output it previously expected from Kamoa-Kakula’s existing plants before operations were disrupted by seismic activity and flooding in May 2025. That adds spending and execution risk as shareholders wait for the operation to recover from last year’s flooding, while leaving the global market with less copper than anticipated. “The path back to about 500,000 tonnes per year has become longer, more capital intensive and more dependent on future execution,” TD Cowen analyst Craig Hutchison wrote Tuesday. He downgraded Ivanhoe to hold from buy and slashed his target price to C$9 ($6.42) from C$14. Ivanhoe had already lowered its 2026 and 2027 output targets in late March after shifting its near-term focus at Kamoa-Kakula from production to underground development, rehabilitation and access work. Shares of Ivanhoe fell 7.2% to C$8.24 Wednesday morning in Toronto, cutting the company’s market capitalization to about C$11.8 billion and extending their drop to 49% since Jan. 1. Earlier they dropped as much as 14% to C$7.64, their lowest level since July 2022. “The revised production and cost guidance over the short term reflects a disciplined approach to the ongoing turnaround at Kamoa-Kakula, prioritizing operational stability, mining flexibility and the sustainable recovery of annualized copper production to approximately 500,000 tonnes,” Friedland, Ivanhoe’s founder and co-chairman, said in the statement. Production mining on Kakula’s eastern side is now expected to begin late in the first quarter of 2028, rather than in next year’s fourth-quarter, Ivanhoe said Tuesday. Ivanhoe also reduced its estimate of Kakula’s maximum mining rate after drilling and engineering studies informed updated geological, groundwater and rock-stability models. The implications stretch beyond next year. Steady-state output from the three existing concentrators is now forecast at 400,000 to 450,000 tonnes annually, compared with a previous outlook exceeding 500,000 tonnes. The plants should be fully utilized from mid-2027 while processing lower-grade ore. Located 1,520 km southeast of the DRC capital Kinshasa, Kamoa-Kakula is one of Africa’s major copper mining sites. Ivanhoe and China’s Zijin Mining each own 39.6% of the operation while the DRC government holds a 20% stake. All production forecasts are on a 100% project basis. Ivanhoe plans to introduce open-pit mining at shallow Kamoa deposits to increase flexibility while Kakula recovers. Initial waste stripping should begin in first-quarter 2027, with first ore in the third quarter. title: US services sector activity cools slightly in October; inflation remains elevated - The Mighty 790 KFGO
body: WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) – US services sector growth slowed marginally in October amid a moderation in new orders, but supply chains remained strained, keeping prices for inputs elevated. The Institute for Supply Management said on Wednesday its nonmanufacturing Purchasing ​Managers’ Index dipped to 54.5 last month from 54.9 in September. A ‌reading above 50 indicates growth in the services sector, which accounts for more than two-thirds of US economic activity. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the PMI little changed at 54.8. The PMI suggested the economy started the fourth quarter on solid footing, though economists expect a slowdown in activity, with consumer ‌spending ​expected to pull back after back-to-back quarters of robust growth. ⁠Spending is seen in part ⁠curbed by high inflation, which is eroding household purchasing power. Income at the disposal of households, after adjusting for inflation and taxes, fell in September after being unchanged in August. The saving rate is at a four-year low of 3.8%. The survey’s measure ​of new orders received by services businesses decreased to 55.9 last month from 59.8 in September. Delivery performance by suppliers deteriorated further against the backdrop of the ongoing ⁠US-Israel war with Iran and tariffs on imports. The ⁠Middle East conflict, now in its ninth month, has boosted energy ​prices and caused shortages of commodities that are shipped through the Strait of Hormuz. The survey’s ​measure of supplier deliveries jumped to 56.7 from 53.2 in September. A ‌reading above 50 indicates slower deliveries. Deliveries have slowed for 23 consecutive months, keeping input prices high. The survey’s measure of prices paid by businesses for inputs eased to a still-high 73.0 last month from 74.0 in September. The ISM on Monday reported a slight moderation in ⁠prices paid for inputs by manufacturers in October. Economists expect inflation to continue to run above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target into 2027. The Fed last Wednesday left its benchmark overnight ⁠interest rate within the 3.75%-4.00% ‌range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated.” Economists expect the US ⁠central bank to raise borrowing costs in December. The ISM survey showed ​a marginal ‌increase in services sector employment, aligning with economists’ expectations for ​moderate growth ⁠in nonfarm payrolls in October. The survey’s measure of services employment rose to 51.4 from 50.1 in September. The government’s closely watched employment report on Friday is likely to show payrolls advanced by 65,000 in October after increasing 29,000 in September, according to a Reuters survey of economists. The unemployment rate is forecast to have been unchanged at 4.2%.

On the September 30 call, President and COO Manish Bhatia called “DRAM the principal constraint versus logic or power to the data center.” Analysts agree: 45 rate the stock a Buy or Strong Buy, with a consensus target of $1,561.91. The bear case falls to $748.96, a 16.33% decline. Memory has always been cyclical, and fiscal 2026 capex of $30.71B could lead to oversupply if AI spending cools. Micron also relies heavily on one lead HBM customer. Management points out that most construction spending is for clean rooms opening in 2028 and beyond, and that equipment goes in only when demand supports it. Sandisk ( NASDAQ:SNDK ) is the closest US-listed memory pure play, with the same exposure to AI storage pricing. The stock changes hands at 17 times trailing earnings, compared with Micron’s 13, even though the two are growing at a similar rate. Western Digital ( NASDAQ:WDC ) also sells storage to hyperscalers, but its hard-drive business grows more slowly and earns lower margins. Micron has the highest margins of the group and trades at a lower earnings multiple than Sandisk. Next to its peers, the 24/7 Wall St. price target looks conservative. The 24/7 Wall St. price target of $995.75 carries a buy rating and 90% confidence. The key factor is contracted demand. I’d stay bullish if HBM4E ramps on schedule and margins hold in the mid-80s. I’d turn cautious if hyperscalers cut capex or contract pricing resets lower. On the evidence so far, Micron’s contracted demand gives it unusual visibility among AI semiconductor stocks. These projections assume Micron keeps running its current strategy. Large moves in either direction could come from HBM4E pricing or a slowdown in AI infrastructure spending. Shares of AI accelerator leader NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) are trading at $202.32, down 2%. Custom-chip designer Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ) is sliding as well; Broadcom stock is at $328.76, down 1%. With the broader market higher, most AI chip stocks are lagging the rebound. The notable exception is AMD, which reported its results after the close on November 3. AMD reported Q3 2026 revenue of $13.38 billion, topping Bloomberg’s consensus estimate of $13.08 billion. On the bottom line, AMD’s adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.09 came in ahead of Bloomberg’s $1.97 consensus estimate. The engine was AMD’s Data Center segment, where revenue reached $8.5 billion, up 97% year over year. CEO Lisa Su said, “Demand for our Instinct and EPYC products continued to strengthen, and we expect growth to accelerate further in the fourth quarter as we scale Helios and Venice production.” During the call, Lisa Su added that AMD expects its revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027. Management at AMD guided its Q4 2026 revenue to approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. Analysts are split on AMD’s valuation after the report. BofA cut its price target to $650 from $720 despite raising its estimates, citing contracting sector multiples. JPMorgan raised its target to $575 from $550 but kept a Neutral rating on the chipmaker. AMD stock is down 22% over the past month, so sentiment was already weak heading into the report. A mix of trimmed targets and a steep run lower helps explain why a strong quarter is producing a measured move. Intel stock is moving lower as its post-earnings slide extends. Shares fell 29% on October 30 after the company guided Q4 revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, short of the $17.29 billion analysts expected. Management at Intel projects an estimated 12% decline in industry PC unit sales in 2026 and a 10% decline in 2027 as memory shortages raise PC prices. That weakness is hiding strength elsewhere, as revenue in Intel’s Data Center and AI segment rose 78% year over year to $7.32 billion. UBS pointed to AMD’s execution relative to Intel, a comparison that’s sharpening as the two chipmakers’ results diverge. AMD designs its chips and relies on outside manufacturers to build them, selling Instinct graphics processing units (GPUs) alongside EPYC server and Ryzen PC processors. Intel takes a different approach, running its own factories through Intel Foundry while it develops its 14A process, which ties its results to heavy manufacturing costs. NVIDIA sells a full-stack AI platform built around its GPUs, networking and CUDA software, and it holds the dominant share of AI accelerators. Broadcom builds custom AI chips and networking silicon for hyperscalers while also selling infrastructure software. Between those models sits AMD, which pitches general-purpose GPUs and rack-scale Helios systems on total cost of ownership.
